title: Quicksort: partition, recursion, and why the worst case is n²
summary: Trace Lomuto partition on paper (pivot, i, j, the final swap, the return value); run quicksort's recursion on an array; write its recurrence and explain the Θ(n²) worst case, the Θ(n log n) best and average case, and how real libraries avoid the worst case.
sourceNote: Lecture 9 slides 'Quicksort' (Sep 21), HW 9 (due Sep 23), CLRS ch. 7. Builds on merge sort (Lecture 5) and recurrences (Lectures 6 and 7).

blocks.md: **The problem with merge sort** Merge sort is always Θ(n log n), but it needs a second array the size of the input to merge into: O(n) extra memory. **Quicksort** sorts *in place*, inside the one array, and on typical inputs it is the fastest comparison sort in practice. That is why it (or a close cousin) is what `Arrays.sort` uses for primitive types in Java and what C's `qsort` is named after.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: **Poon's analogy: sorting by height** Pick one student as the **pivot**. Everyone shorter moves to their left, everyone taller to their right. The pivot is now standing exactly where they would be in a fully sorted line, even though the two groups are still messy. Now do the same thing inside each group. When every group is size 0 or 1, the whole line is sorted.

blocks.body: The one element chosen to split the array. After partitioning, smaller-or-equal elements are to its left, larger to its right, and **the pivot is in its final sorted position**. In this lecture the pivot is always the **last** element of the part being sorted (this is called **Lomuto** quicksort).

sections.heading: partition: the one step that does all the work

blocks.body: Works only on `a[low..high]`. Picks `pivot = a[high]`, moves every element ≤ pivot to the left part, puts the pivot right after them, and **returns the pivot's new index**.

blocks.title: The pseudocode (Lecture 9)
blocks.body:
partition(a, low, high):
    pivot = a[high]
    i = low - 1              // zone of '≤ pivot' is empty
    for j = low to high - 1  // j scouts, skips pivot
        if a[j] <= pivot
            i++              // grow the zone
            swap a[i] with a[j]  // pull it in
    swap a[i+1] with a[high] // pivot after zone
    return i + 1

blocks.md: Two markers do the work. **j is the scout**: it walks left to right over every element except the pivot. **i is the boundary**: everything from `low` to `i` is known to be ≤ pivot. When the scout finds a small element, the boundary grows by one and the small element is swapped into the new spot. Big elements are simply walked past; they end up between the boundary and the scout.

frames.caption: partition(a, 0, 4). The pivot is the last element, a[4] = 5. i starts at −1: the '≤ pivot' zone is empty. j (the scout) starts at 0.
j = 0: is 9 ≤ 5? No. Skip it. i stays −1.
j = 1: is 3 ≤ 5? Yes. i++ → 0, then swap a[0] and a[1]. The 3 moves into the '≤ pivot' zone, which is now a[0..0].
j = 2: is 1 ≤ 5? Yes. i++ → 1, swap a[1] and a[2]. The zone a[0..1] = 3, 1 holds everything small so far.
j = 3: is 7 ≤ 5? No. Skip. The loop stops before high, so we are done scouting.
Last step: swap a[i+1] = a[2] with the pivot a[4]. The 5 lands at index 2, its final sorted place. Return 2.

blocks.caption: Pick *quicksort* and press Next to watch every partition step. Then type your own array. Try an already sorted one like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and count the comparisons.

blocks.md: **Runtime of partition** The loop runs once for each element from `low` to `high − 1`, doing constant work each time. So partition on n elements is **Θ(n)**.

blocks.body: Returning i instead of i + 1. After the loop, i points at the last small element; the pivot goes one to the right of it, at i + 1, and that is what partition returns.

Counting indexes from `low` instead of from 0. partition returns an index into the **whole** array. On the slide's 'Your turn' (a = [19, 9, 5, 1, 8, 7, 2, 3, 4, 6], low = 2, high = 7), the pivot is a[7] = 3 and it lands at **index 4** of the whole array. The slide's answer says 'index 3' because its picture starts at a[1]; when you write your own answer, count from a[0].

blocks.prompt: partition([4, 8, 2, 6, 5], 0, 4): what is the array afterwards, and what is returned?
blocks.answer: Pivot 5. j=0: 4 ≤ 5, i=0 (swap with itself). j=1: 8 skip. j=2: 2 ≤ 5, i=1, swap → [4, 2, 8, 6, 5]. j=3: 6 skip. Final swap a[2] ↔ a[4] → [4, 2, 5, 6, 8]. Return 2.

sections.heading: quicksort: partition, then recurse on both sides

blocks.title: The pseudocode
blocks.body:
quicksort(a, low, high):
    if low < high                  // 2+ elements
        p = partition(a, low, high) // p is final
        quicksort(a, low, p - 1)    // left side
        quicksort(a, p + 1, high)   // right side

First call: quicksort(a, 0, n - 1)

blocks.md: Notice what is **not** there: no merge step. Once the pivot is in place and both sides are sorted, the whole range is sorted, because every left element ≤ pivot < every right element. And the pivot is **excluded** from both recursive calls (p − 1 and p + 1): it is already done.

frames.caption: Sort the whole array. low = 0 < high = 7, so partition.
Pivot 4 lands at index 3. Everything left of it is ≤ 4, everything right is > 4. Index 3 is finished forever.
Recurse on the left part, indexes 0 to 2. Pivot 3 is already the biggest, so it stays at index 2.
Left of that: [2, 1] with pivot 1. It moves to index 0.
Base case: low ≥ high means 0 or 1 elements. Nothing to sort. This is where the recursion stops.
Now the right side of the first pivot. The same three lines, over and over, until every element has been a pivot or a base case.
Sorted, in place. There was never a merge step: once both sides are sorted around the pivot, the whole thing is sorted.

blocks.md: That table is the one idea to remember: merge sort does its work on the way **up** (merging), quicksort does its work on the way **down** (partitioning).

blocks.prompt: In quicksort(a, low, high), why is the base case `low < high` and not `low <= high`?
blocks.answer: When low = high there is one element, and one element is already sorted. When low > high the range is empty. Both mean: nothing to do.

sections.heading: How fast? It depends on the pivot

blocks.title: The recurrence
blocks.body:
Let q = size of the left side after partition.
The right side has n − q − 1 (the pivot is in neither).

T(n) = T(q) + T(n − q − 1) + Θ(n)
                              └ partition

blocks.md: Unlike merge sort, **q is not fixed**. It depends on where the pivot lands, which depends on the data. So there is no single recurrence; there is a best one and a worst one.

blocks.title: Worst case: the input is already sorted
blocks.body:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The pivot (last) is always the biggest.
Left side gets n − 1 elements, right side gets 0.

T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(0) + Θ(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n)
     = n + (n − 1) + … + 2 + 1
     = n(n + 1)/2 = Θ(n²)

blocks.title: Best case: the pivot lands in the middle every time
blocks.body:
Both sides get about n/2.

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)

That is exactly merge sort's recurrence. Master method case 2 → Θ(n log n).

blocks.md: **Average case** On random input the splits are uneven but not terrible, and quicksort is still **Θ(n log n)**. Even a lopsided 9-to-1 split at every level gives Θ(n log n): the tree is deeper (log base 10/9 instead of 2) but still logarithmic, and each level still costs Θ(n). CLRS 7.4 has the proof.

blocks.title: The three n log n sorts (Lecture 9 slide 31)
blocks.slide: Quicksort vs merge sort vs heap sort

blocks.body: Saying quicksort's worst case is n log n, or that it happens on random input. The worst case is Θ(n²), and for Lomuto it happens on **already sorted** (or reverse sorted) input, the input you would think is easiest.

blocks.prompt: Why does quicksort use O(log n) extra space if it sorts in place?
blocks.answer: The recursion itself: each pending call sits on the call stack. With balanced splits the recursion is about log n deep. (In the worst case it is n deep.)

sections.heading: How real code avoids the worst case

blocks.md: Nobody ships the version from class as-is: one sorted input and it crawls. Real implementations change **how the pivot is chosen** or **how partition works**.

rows: pick a random index, swap it to the end, then partition as usual
sorted input no longer means bad pivots; the n² case becomes astronomically unlikely
pivot = median of first, middle, last
a sorted array now gets a perfect middle pivot
two markers start at both ends and walk toward each other, swapping out-of-place pairs
fewer swaps than Lomuto on average
blocks.title: Three fixes (Lecture 9 slide 33)

blocks.md: **Where you will meet this** Java's `Arrays.sort(int[])` is a dual-pivot quicksort; C's `qsort` and C++'s `std::sort` are quicksort hybrids that switch to insertion sort on small pieces (the same trick as your Project 1 hybrid) and to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep. Interviewers ask for `partition` constantly because it tests loops, indexes and invariants in ten lines.

blocks.prompt: Randomizing the pivot changes the worst-case running time to what?
blocks.answer: Nothing: the worst case is still O(n²) (an unlucky random pick every time). What changes is that no particular input causes it, so the **expected** time on every input is Θ(n log n).

exercises.title: Trace partition yourself
exercises.prompt: Run partition(a, 0, 5) on a = [6, 2, 9, 1, 7, 4]. Write the array after every swap, the final array, and the return value.
hints: pivot = a[5] = 4. i starts at −1. j goes from 0 to 4.
Only 2 and 1 are ≤ 4. Each time you find one: i++, then swap a[i] and a[j].
After the loop, swap a[i+1] with a[5]. What is i at that point?
exercises.why: Tracing is how Poon tests partition, and it is exactly what HW 9 Question 1 asks for on a longer array.

exercises.title: Pick the worst input
exercises.prompt: Which input makes Lomuto quicksort (pivot = last element) take Θ(n²) time?
hints: Bad means the pivot keeps landing at one end.
Where does the pivot land if it is the largest element?
Which common input makes the last element the largest in every subarray?
solution: If the array is sorted, the last element is the maximum, so every partition puts n − 1 elements on the left and 0 on the right.
exercises.why: Sorted data is extremely common in real systems (data that is appended in time order, for one), which is exactly why no library ships plain Lomuto.

choices.feedback: Right. The pivot is always the max, so each call only peels off one element.
Random input gives Θ(n log n) on average: splits are uneven but not consistently terrible.

choices.text: An array where every element is different
choices.feedback: Distinct values don't matter by themselves; the order does.

exercises.title: Write partition in Java (HW 9 Question 2)
exercises.prompt: Write `public static int partition(int[] a, int low, int high)` from the pseudocode, with a `swap` helper. Test it on the example above: partition(new int[]{9, 3, 1, 7, 5}, 0, 4) must return 2 and leave the array as [3, 1, 5, 7, 9].
hints: Translate line by line. `pivot = a[high]`, `i = low - 1`, a for loop with `j < high` (not ≤).
The swap helper: `int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;`
Check the two classic slips: the loop must stop before `high`, and the method returns `i + 1`.
solution: Declare pivot and i from the first two pseudocode lines.
for (int j = low; j < high; j++) with the if / i++ / swap inside.
After the loop: swap(a, i + 1, high); return i + 1;
Run the test: print the array with Arrays.toString and the returned index.
exercises.why: Writing it once from scratch is the fastest way to make the i/j invariant stick, and partition is one of the most-asked interview snippets.
